I used to be able to keep a level head, but lately, the financial pressure has just felt completely overwhelming.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'not handling the money stress in a normal way' - are you experiencing persistent worries, fears, or physical symptoms like a racing heart or difficulty sleeping?\n\nPatient: I don't really have physical symptoms like a racing heart or trouble sleeping, but I feel mentally overwhelmed and scattered. I keep bouncing between panicking about my rent, snapping at my partner over tiny things, and then just zoning out and avoiding my bills entirely.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'zoning out and avoiding my bills entirely' - are you avoiding thinking about or dealing with your financial problems as a way of coping with the stress?\n\nPatient: Yes, exactly. Going to those sketching circles and galleries just reminds me of my stalled career plans, which makes me feel too overwhelmed to show up right now. I still want to do those things, but I just can't bring myself to face them in my current situation.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant distress or impairment in your daily life, relationships, or work, beyond just the financial stress and avoidance behaviors you've described?\n\nPatient: No, the difficulties are really just concentrated on the things I've already mentioned. Outside of those specific reactions to this money stress, there isn't really any other major impairment.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've experienced any intense fear or anxiety episodes that come on suddenly, such as panic attacks, or if your anxiety has been more of a constant, low-grade feeling in response to your financial situation?\n\nPatient: It's definitely not sudden, unprovoked panic attacks, but rather a constant, overwhelming stress tied directly to my financial situation. I just find myself constantly bouncing between spiraling and panicking about my rent, and then zoning out to ignore the bills entirely.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced this level of anxiety or avoidance behaviors in response to other stressful situations in the past, or is this primarily triggered by your current financial difficulties?\n\nPatient: No, this level of anxiety and avoidance is completely new to me and is directly triggered by suddenly losing my gallery income. I've never handled stress this way in the past, and I really expect that once my financial situation stabilizes, these feelings will ease up.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that this level of anxiety and avoidance is new to you and triggered by your current financial situation, but can you think of any other significant life events or stressors in the past that you handled without experiencing this level of distress or avoidance?\n\nPatient: I haven't really faced a major setback like this before in my life. Usually, I manage to stay relatively calm and just figure things out as they come, which is why this current reaction feels so incredibly new and overwhelming to me.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your current financial situation is the trigger for your anxiety and avoidance behaviors, but can you tell me if you're experiencing any intrusive thoughts, memories, or flashbacks related to the loss of your gallery income, or is it purely the practical stress of the situation that's affecting you?\n\nPatient: No, I'm not having any flashbacks or intrusive memories about the gallery closing itself. My distress is entirely about the practical consequences, like the constant worry over paying rent, falling behind on bills, and the stress of trying to find new income so I don't get evicted.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety and avoidance behaviors are primarily focused on the fear of a specific outcome, such as losing your home or not being able to provide for yourself, or is it more about the general uncertainty and unpredictability of your financial situation?\n\nPatient: It’s really a combination of both, but the specific fear of losing my home is what triggers my panic the most, especially after a tense meeting with my landlord about a potential eviction warning. That immediate threat, combined with the general uncertainty of my income, makes me so overwhelmed that I just shut down and avoid looking at the bills altogether.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your anxiety and avoidance behaviors would significantly decrease if your financial situation were to immediately stabilize, such as receiving a new source of income or resolving your debt, or if you think other factors would still contribute to your anxiety?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. I'm confident that if my financial situation stabilized, this anxiety and avoidance would almost completely go away. It really feels entirely tied to this money crunch, and I expect these feelings to ease up once I secure a steady part-time job or a new income stream.\n\nDoctor: If you were to secure a new job or a stable financial solution tomorrow, do you think your anxiety and avoidance behaviors would resolve quickly, or do you think it would take some time for you to adjust and feel back to normal?\n\nPatient: I really believe I would feel back to normal pretty quickly. Since all of this anxiety is directly tied to the current financial pressure, resolving that would lift the weight off me almost immediately. I don't think these feelings would drag on once I have a steady income stream again.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your symptoms are directly tied to your financial situation, but can you imagine experiencing similar anxiety or avoidance if you were facing a different kind of significant stressor, such as a health issue or a relationship problem, or do you think your reaction would be significantly different in those cases?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure, and I haven't thought about how I'd react to other stressors like that. My current distress feels very specifically tied to this sudden financial crisis and the threat of eviction. It's just hard to imagine anything else right now when this money situation is what's consuming me.\n\nDoctor: If you were to experience a different significant stressor, such as a serious health issue or the end of a relationship, do you think you would react with a similar level of anxiety and avoidance, or do you believe your response would be more adaptive and less overwhelming?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure how I would react to other hypothetical stressors like a health issue or a breakup, as I haven't really thought about it. Right now, my focus is entirely on this current financial stress because it feels so uniquely overwhelming compared to how I normally handle things.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that your current anxiety and avoidance behaviors are exclusively related to the financial stress, or could other significant life stressors potentially trigger a similar reaction in the future?"

That immediate threat, combined with the general uncertainty of my income, makes me so overwhelmed that I just shut down and avoid looking at the bills altogether.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your anxiety and avoidance behaviors would significantly decrease if your financial situation were to immediately stabilize, such as receiving a new source of income or resolving your debt, or if you think other factors would still contribute to your anxiety?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. That immediate threat, combined with the general uncertainty of my income, makes me so overwhelmed that I just shut down and avoid looking at the bills altogether.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your anxiety and avoidance behaviors would significantly decrease if your financial situation were to immediately stabilize, such as receiving a new source of income or resolving your debt, or if you think other factors would still contribute to your anxiety?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. I'm confident that if my financial situation stabilized, this anxiety and avoidance would almost completely go away. It really feels entirely tied to this money crunch, and I expect these feelings to ease up once I secure a steady part-time job or a new income stream.\n\nDoctor: If you were to secure a new job or a stable financial solution tomorrow, do you think your anxiety and avoidance behaviors would resolve quickly, or do you think it would take some time for you to adjust and feel back to normal?\n\nPatient: I really believe I would feel back to normal pretty quickly. Since all of this anxiety is directly tied to the current financial pressure, resolving that would lift the weight off me almost immediately. I don't think these feelings would drag on once I have a steady income stream again.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your symptoms are directly tied to your financial situation, but can you imagine experiencing similar anxiety or avoidance if you were facing a different kind of significant stressor, such as a health issue or a relationship problem, or do you think your reaction would be significantly different in those cases?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure, and I haven't thought about how I'd react to other stressors like that. My current distress feels very specifically tied to this sudden financial crisis and the threat of eviction. It's just hard to imagine anything else right now when this money situation is what's consuming me.\n\nDoctor: If you were to experience a different significant stressor, such as a serious health issue or the end of a relationship, do you think you would react with a similar level of anxiety and avoidance, or do you believe your response would be more adaptive and less overwhelming?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure how I would react to other hypothetical stressors like a health issue or a breakup, as I haven't really thought about it.
